query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a sacrificial alloying element (e.g., aluminum) into steels used in molten chloride salt environments creates a redox buffer (via the Al/AlCl3 couple) that suppresses chromium dissolution and, therefore, enhances corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual-phase structural steels, such as conventional DS2205 duplex stainless steel, compared with a modified steel that includes an increased aluminum content to act sacrificially.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by incorporating aluminum as a sacrificial element.
generation.conditions: Exposure in a molten salt environment (using a NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 eutectic mixture) at controlled temperatures (450 °C and 650 °C) under laboratory corrosion tests.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a redox buffer at the alloy/salt interface through the preferential oxidation of aluminum forming AlCl3, which regulates the local redox potential.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum preferentially oxidizes to form AlCl3, establishing an Al/AlCl3 redox couple that reduces the effective corrosion potential of the salt. This buffering makes chromium dissolution thermodynamically unfavorable, thereby preserving the protective Cr content in the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels with added aluminum will demonstrate a significantly lower chromium depletion depth and reduced overall corrosion rate compared to baseline steels without the sacrificial element, as evidenced by a more stable and less depleted corrosion layer.
generation.baseline: Benchmark steels that do not contain or are low in sacrificial elements (e.g., standard DS2205 duplex stainless steel) under the same molten salt exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesized mechanism is expected to hold in high-temperature molten chloride salt environments (450 °C to 650 °C) typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications; its applicability to aqueous or other salt chemistries remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of chromium protection and reduction in corrosion rates depends on the precise aluminum content, microstructural factors, and any variations in salt composition or impurities. Quantitative differences may vary and require further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled study wherein two groups of steels are prepared: one group with a conventional DS2205 composition (or similar alloy lacking significant sacrificial elements) and another modified by adding aluminum. Both groups are exposed to molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 at 450 °C and 650 °C for identical time periods. Post-exposure, assess corrosion morphology using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), measure chromium depletion depths via energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and determine the molten salt’s redox potential before and after exposure.
measurements: Chromium depletion depth via cross-sectional SEM/EDS analysis
Overall corrosion rates using weight loss measurements
Redox potential of the molten salt
Phase composition and integrity of the corrosion layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If steels with aluminum addition do not show a statistically significant reduction in chromium depletion depth and overall corrosion rate compared to the control group, or if no evidence of a redox buffering effect (i.e., a shift in redox potential) is observed, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].

chosen.approach: Redox buffering using sacrificial/diffusing elements in molten salts
